question.text:
A portfolio manager is analyzing the performance of a mixed-asset portfolio consisting of 40% equities, 40% bonds, and 20% commodities. The expected return of equities is 10%, bonds is 5%, and commodities is 8%. The standard deviation of equities is 12%, bonds is 6%, and commodities is 10%. The risk-free rate is 3%. The correlations between the asset classes are as follows: equities and bonds: 0.2, equities and commodities: 0.4, bonds and commodities: 0.3.
Which asset class contributes the most to the portfolio's risk?

explanation.text: The Logic: Portfolio risk depends on individual standard deviations, weights, and pairwise correlations. Equities carry both the largest weight tied with bonds (40%) and the highest individual standard deviation (12%), so the equity sleeve dominates the covariance-weighted sum and contributes the most to portfolio risk. The Trap: Bonds and commodities tempt candidates who focus on either the smaller weight or the lower-but-still-meaningful standard deviation of commodities. "All contribute equally" tempts those who assume equal weighting yields equal risk contribution, which ignores the standard-deviation differences and correlations. Note: The dependence of portfolio risk on weights, standard deviations, and correlations is set out in the source workbook on the cited page.
